questions.stem: Which statement defines diffusion?

options.text: Net spreading of particles from where they are more concentrated towards where they are less concentrated
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Movement of water through a partially permeable membrane
options.explanation: That defines osmosis, a special case of water movement.

options.text: Movement of particles against their gradient using energy
options.explanation: That describes active transport, not diffusion.

options.text: Movement of particles driven by cell energy expenditure
options.explanation: Diffusion costs the cell nothing.

questions.stem: Why is diffusion described as a passive process?

options.text: Because respiration powers it
options.explanation: Respiration powers active transport, not diffusion.

options.text: The particles' own kinetic energy drives the spreading, so the cell spends nothing
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because it only happens in dead cells
options.explanation: Diffusion happens in living cells constantly.

options.text: Because the membrane forces particles through
options.explanation: The membrane only gates what may cross.

questions.stem: Oxygen crosses a cell membrane but starch does not. Which property explains this?

options.text: Starch particles move too slowly
options.explanation: Speed is not what keeps starch out; size and the membrane are.

options.text: Oxygen is actively transported in
options.explanation: Oxygen diffuses freely down its gradient.

options.text: The membrane is partially permeable, admitting small molecules and blocking large ones
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The membrane is fully permeable to everything
options.explanation: If so, starch would cross too.

questions.stem: During photosynthesis, why does carbon dioxide enter leaf cells?

options.text: Because leaf cells pump it in against its gradient
options.explanation: No energy is spent; the gradient does the work.

options.text: Because the leaf is warmer than the air
options.explanation: Temperature is not what drives entry here.

options.text: Because water carries it in by osmosis
options.explanation: Osmosis moves water, not carbon dioxide.

options.text: Its concentration inside the chloroplasts is lower than in the surrounding air
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: Which example correctly pairs an organ with the substance diffusing there?

options.text: Liver — urea leaving its cells into the blood
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Liver — oxygen entering its cells
options.explanation: The liver example is waste urea leaving.

options.text: Lungs — carbon dioxide entering the blood
options.explanation: In the lungs, oxygen enters the blood; carbon dioxide leaves.

options.text: Leaf — starch leaving the mesophyll
options.explanation: Starch is too large to diffuse out of leaf cells.

questions.stem: State the direction particles travel during diffusion.
questions.modelAnswer: They travel down the concentration gradient, from higher to lower concentration.

questions.stem: Give one example of diffusion in a living organism.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen diffusing from the alveoli into the blood in the lungs.

questions.stem: Explain why diffusion stops once particles are evenly spread.
questions.modelAnswer: With no concentration difference left there is no gradient to drive a net flow; individual particles keep moving randomly, but equal numbers cross any boundary in both directions, so the overall spread no longer changes.

questions.stem: A student opens a scent bottle at the front of the lab. Predict and explain where the smell will be strongest after ten minutes.
questions.modelAnswer: Strongest at the bottle, because particles diffuse from that region of higher concentration outwards down the gradient, and after ten minutes the far corners have received fewer particles than the air beside the source.

questions.stem: Which definition of osmosis earns full credit?

options.text: Evaporation of water from a leaf surface
options.explanation: That is transpiration, not osmosis.

options.text: Water diffusing across a partially permeable membrane, from the dilute side towards the concentrated one
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Movement of any solute through a membrane
options.explanation: Osmosis concerns water alone.

options.text: Movement of water against its gradient using energy
options.explanation: Osmosis is passive and runs down the gradient.

questions.stem: What happens to an animal cell placed in distilled water?

options.text: It stays exactly the same
options.explanation: A gradient exists, so net movement occurs.

options.text: It pumps the water back out using energy
options.explanation: Animal cells do not reverse osmosis by pumping.

options.text: It gains water and may burst, because it lacks a cell wall
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It shrivels as water leaves
options.explanation: Distilled water is the dilute side; water enters.

questions.stem: A red blood cell in a strong sugar solution becomes crenated. What caused this?

options.text: Sugar entered the cell by osmosis
options.explanation: The membrane blocks larger solutes like sugar.

options.text: The cell produced water by respiration
options.explanation: Respiration uses water; it does not cause the shrinkage.

options.text: The cell wall squeezed the cell
options.explanation: Animal cells have no cell wall.

options.text: Water left the cell, moving towards the lower water concentration outside
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: How does dissolved salt change a solution's water potential?

options.text: It lowers the potential, and the more solute the lower it falls
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It raises the potential
options.explanation: Solutes pull potential down, not up.

options.text: It has no effect on potential
options.explanation: Potential depends directly on solute concentration.

options.text: It makes potential equal to pure water
options.explanation: Pure water alone holds the highest potential.

questions.stem: Why do sugars stay on their own side of an osmosis membrane?

options.text: Sugar molecules evaporate
options.explanation: Sugars are non-volatile solutes.

options.text: The partially permeable membrane blocks larger molecules while water passes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Sugars lack the energy to move
options.explanation: Sugars share the same kinetic energy as water.

options.text: Sugars are actively pumped away
options.explanation: No transport is involved; the membrane simply excludes them.

questions.stem: State the term for water moving from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a membrane.
questions.modelAnswer: That movement is osmosis — water diffusing across a partially permeable membrane towards the concentrated side.

questions.stem: Name the shrivelled state of an animal cell that has lost water.
questions.modelAnswer: The cell is described as crenated, meaning shrivelled after water loss.

questions.stem: Explain why pure water has the highest water potential.
questions.modelAnswer: Because potential falls as solute is added, and pure water contains no dissolved solute at all, so nothing pulls its value down — every other solution sits lower on the scale.

questions.stem: A patient is given an intravenous drip. Explain why the fluid must match blood concentration.
questions.modelAnswer: If the drip fluid were too dilute, water would osmose into the red cells and could burst them; if too concentrated, water would leave and crenate them, so the fluid is matched to the blood to keep the cells' water balance steady.

questions.stem: What prevents a plant cell from bursting in distilled water?

options.text: The cell stops osmosis by using energy
options.explanation: Osmosis continues; the wall simply resists the swell.

options.text: The shrinkage of the vacuole
options.explanation: In distilled water the vacuole expands, not shrinks.

options.text: Its inelastic cellulose wall, which the swelling membrane pushes against
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: A contractile vacuole that pumps water out
options.explanation: That is a single-celled freshwater adaptation, not a wall.

questions.stem: Which term describes a plant cell whose membrane has pulled away from its wall?

options.text: Crenated
options.explanation: Crenation describes shrivelled animal cells.

options.text: Turgid
options.explanation: Turgid cells are swollen, not shrunken.

options.text: Lysed
options.explanation: Lysis means bursting, which walls prevent.

options.text: Plasmolysed
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which statement defines active transport?

options.text: Movement of particles across the membrane from lower to higher concentration, using energy from respiration
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Movement down a gradient through a membrane
options.explanation: That is diffusion.

options.text: Water movement across a partially permeable membrane
options.explanation: That is osmosis.

options.text: Movement of particles without any energy cost
options.explanation: Active transport is precisely the energy-costing route.

questions.stem: Where does the energy for active transport come from?

options.text: The sodium hydroxide in the solution
options.explanation: Unrelated chemistry.

options.text: Respiration inside the cell
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The kinetic energy of the particles
options.explanation: That energy powers passive diffusion.

options.text: Sunlight absorbed directly by the membrane
options.explanation: Light is not the direct cell-level source here.

questions.stem: Which structure actually carries particles during active transport?

options.text: The vacuole
options.explanation: It stores sap; it does not pump across the membrane.

options.text: Chloroplasts
options.explanation: They photosynthesise; transport pumps live in the membrane.

options.text: Protein pumps embedded in the cell membrane
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The cellulose wall
options.explanation: The wall is outside the membrane and passive.

questions.stem: Name the state of a plant cell that is swollen and firm.
questions.modelAnswer: The cell is turgid, pressed firm against its wall by the swollen vacuole.

questions.stem: Give one example of active transport in a plant cell.
questions.modelAnswer: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from the soil against their concentration gradient.

questions.stem: Explain why turgid cells stop a seedling from wilting.
questions.modelAnswer: Because each turgid cell presses outward against its wall, and the combined pressure stiffens the tissues; when water is scarce the cells lose turgor, the tissue slackens and the seedling wilts.

questions.stem: A farmer fertilises soil where mineral ions sit at lower concentration than in root cells. Explain how roots still absorb them.
questions.modelAnswer: The ions must move against their gradient, so the root hair cells spend energy released by respiration and use protein pumps to run active transport, pulling the ions in despite the unfavourable direction.
